# A normal-preserving boundary coupling from localized convex order

This note supplies the transport consequence of equations (10)--(11) in
`candidate a68c14b477a24d06`. The transport theorem
below is proved independently of that variational argument. Applying it to
a depth minimum is conditional on the hypotheses proved in that separate
note. Neither note proves the numerical OC inequality.

All measures below are finite nonnegative Borel measures on finite-dimensional
Euclidean compact sets. Equal-mass convex order, written nu <=cx mu, means
integral Phi dnu <= integral Phi dmu for every finite continuous convex
function Phi on the ambient Euclidean space, and equality of total masses.
Affine tests then give equality of first moments. A zero-mass case always
has the zero coupling and can be omitted.

## 1. Finite convex order has a barycenter-preserving coupling

Suppose nu=sum_i m_i delta_(x_i) and mu=sum_j n_j delta_(y_j), with positive
listed masses, and nu <=cx mu. Then there are t_ij>=0 with

    sum_j t_ij=m_i,       sum_i t_ij=n_j,
    sum_j t_ij y_j=m_i x_i.                              (1)

First, every x_i is in conv{y_j}. Indeed the distance to that convex hull
is a nonnegative continuous convex function, zero mu-almost everywhere;
convex order forces it to be zero at each positive nu-atom.

Consider the compact nonempty polytope of arrays satisfying the row sums
and row barycenters in (1), without prescribing their column sums. Its
image T under the column-sum map is compact convex. If n is outside T,
finite-dimensional strict separation, reversing the separator if needed,
gives b in R^J with

    sum_j b_j n_j < min_(s in T) sum_j b_j s_j.           (2)

On conv{y_j} put

    f(x)=min{sum_j alpha_j b_j: alpha>=0,
                 sum alpha=1, sum alpha_j y_j=x}.

The minimum is attained. This function is convex and piecewise affine.
For completeness, its epigraph over conv{y_j} is the convex hull of the
vertical rays starting at (y_j,b_j). The nonvertical lower facets of this
polyhedron represent f as a finite maximum of affine functions on the
affine span of conv{y_j}. Extend those affine functions to the whole
ambient space and take their maximum, obtaining a finite continuous
convex extension, still called f. In dimension zero the constant extension
suffices. At every y_j one has f(y_j)<=b_j.

Independent minimization of the rows gives the right side of (2) as
sum_i m_i f(x_i). But convex order gives

    sum_i m_i f(x_i) <= sum_j n_j f(y_j) <= sum_j n_j b_j,

contradicting (2). Therefore n is in T, proving (1).

## 2. Compact convex order has a barycenter-preserving coupling

For arbitrary compactly supported nu <=cx mu, there exists a finite measure
pi on pairs (x,y), with first marginal nu and second marginal mu, such that

    integral f(x)(y-x) dpi(x,y)=0                       (3)

for every bounded Borel scalar function f. Vector equality is coordinatewise.

Here is a finite approximation proof. For a grid of mesh delta, replace
the restriction of nu to each occupied half-open grid cube by its total
mass at its conditional barycenter. This gives a finite measure nu_delta.
Jensen's inequality proves nu_delta <=cx nu, and nu_delta converges weakly
to nu as delta tends to zero; displacement in this replacement is at most
sqrt(k) delta in ambient dimension k.

For mu use the reverse construction: split each point y among the vertices
of its enclosing grid cube with the usual multilinear coordinate weights.
These weights are nonnegative, sum to one, and have barycenter y. Integrate
them against mu to obtain a finite measure mu_delta^+. Thus mu <=cx
mu_delta^+, and mu_delta^+ converges weakly to mu. Use one fixed convention
on grid boundaries. All measures remain in one fixed compact box.

Transitivity gives nu_delta <=cx mu_delta^+. Section 1 gives finite
couplings pi_delta with their row barycenters fixed. A weakly convergent
subsequence exists in the fixed compact product box, since the total mass
is fixed. Its limit pi has the required marginals. For continuous f the
integrand in (3) is continuous and bounded, so (3) passes to the limit.
For each coordinate of y-x this says that a finite signed Borel measure
on the x-space integrates every continuous function to zero. That measure
is zero; hence (3) holds for every bounded Borel f. This proves the claim
without invoking a general martingale transport theorem.

## 3. Localized convex order can preserve a compact parameter exactly

Let U be a compact metric space and X a compact subset of R^k. Suppose
eta and nu are finite measures on U times X, supported on a compact
relation N subset U times X, with the following properties:

* Their U-coordinate is a Borel function n(x) of their X-coordinate,
  outside one null set for both measures.
* For every continuous psi on U and every affine A on R^k,

      integral psi(u) A(x) d(eta-nu)(u,x)=0.           (4)

* For every continuous psi>=0 and every finite continuous convex Phi,

      integral psi(u) Phi(x) d(eta-nu)(u,x)>=0.        (5)

Then there is a coupling Pi of nu to eta, on N times N, such that

    u=v Pi-almost everywhere,
    integral f(u,x)(y-x) dPi((u,x),(v,y))=0            (6)

for every bounded Borel f on N.

To prove it, fix a Borel subset B of U. For each affine A, the signed
measure on U obtained by integrating A against eta-nu is zero by (4).
For each convex Phi the corresponding signed measure is nonnegative by
(5), since nonnegativity against all continuous nonnegative tests
characterizes positive Borel measures on a compact metric space.
Consequently the physical marginals nu_B and eta_B of the restrictions
to B times X have equal masses and nu_B <=cx eta_B. This statement holds
for every B and every convex test; no exceptional parameter choices are
discarded.

Partition U into finitely many Borel sets of diameter at most delta.
Section 2 gives a physical coupling of nu_B to eta_B in each cell. Its
marginals are concentrated where n is defined. Lift it by

    (x,y) -> ((n(x),x),(n(y),y)).

Both parameter values lie in the same cell almost everywhere. The lifted
coupling has the normal-bundle marginals restricted to that cell. Because
(3) holds for every bounded Borel test, it also holds with f(n(x),x).
Summing over the cells gives a coupling Pi_delta of nu to eta, supported
on N times N, with distance(u,v)<=delta almost everywhere and the second
identity in (6) for all bounded Borel tests.

Take a weakly convergent subsequence in the compact space N times N. The
limit retains the marginals. The continuous nonnegative parameter-distance
function has integrals tending to zero, proving u=v in the limit. The
moment identities pass to the limit for continuous f on N, and the same
signed-measure argument as in Section 2 extends them to all bounded Borel
f. This proves (6). No parameter-dependent measurable choice of individual
couplings, disintegrations, or linear-programming bases is needed.

## 4. Application to arbitrary convex fiber boundaries

Let P be finite and let every K_p be a positive d-dimensional convex body,
d>=1. Let

    N={(u,p,x): |u|=1, x in K_p, u.x=h_(K_p)(u)}.

This is compact. Let eta be the sum over p of boundary H_(d-1), marked
with its unique outer normal at regular boundary points. For d=1 the
two endpoints have their respective normals and H_0 is used. In higher
dimensions the nonregular boundary set is surface-null; Lipschitz graph
charts give both this fact and Borel measurability of the normal map.
The base index distinguishes physical points from different fibers.

Suppose a nonnegative measure nu, absolutely continuous with respect to
eta, satisfies (4)--(5) with physical variable w=(p,x). Section 3 gives
a coupling Pi from nu to eta preserving its continuous outer normal and
having full physical row barycenter w. In particular, for every bounded
Borel f(u,p,x),

    integral f(u,p,x)(q-p) dPi=0,
    integral f(u,p,x)(y-x) dPi=0.                       (7)

These equalities retain the continuous coordinates, not just the integer
base moments. They do not change or round the base set.

For clarity one can express their support implication using conditional
probabilities. On a compact Euclidean space a finite measure admits regular
conditional distributions with respect to its first coordinate. Equivalently,
the following row assertions are precisely the moment identities (7).
For nu-almost every input (u,p,x), the output row is supported on
(u,q,y) with y in K_q and u.y=h_q(u), and has mean (p,x). Writing its
base probabilities as alpha_q gives

    sum_q alpha_q q=p,
    sum_q alpha_q h_q(u)=u.x=h_p(u).                    (8)

Thus, if the fibers are actual compatible sections, every transported row
uses an ACTIVE anchored support equality. Any continuous spreading in an
output fiber remains within that fiber's exposed face at the same normal.
One may use (7) throughout instead of invoking conditional distributions.

At the variational minimum of the source note,

    dnu=(sum_j lambda_j alpha_j) deta,
    sum_j lambda_j=1/beta,

where alpha_j is the strict cap trace off coincident facets and is the
consistent branch allocation on a coincident facet. If that source note's
necessary conditions hold, the present theorem therefore constructs an
actual normal-preserving boundary coupling for each selected critical cap
cover. It does not infer a coupling of mixed-integer volume, a selected
center of S, or a lower bound for beta. Those are additional mathematical
claims and remain to be proved.

## 5. For actual fibers, global physical convex order already preserves normals

There is a useful simplification in the particular geometric application.
Suppose the K_p are ACTUAL sections of their convex hull C, and nu and eta
are both concentrated on their regular fiber boundaries. If their physical
marginals satisfy nu <=cx eta, any barycenter-preserving physical coupling
from Section 2 preserves the continuous outer normal almost everywhere.
Thus in this setting the normal-localized convex-order conclusion follows
already from global physical convex order; it is not an additional
independent strength of the certificate.

Here are the supporting-plane and measurability details. Fix a unit u.
The section support function on B=conv(P) is the finite linear-programming
roof

    h_z(u)=max{sum alpha_q h_q(u):sum alpha=1,
                                  sum alpha_q q=z, alpha>=0}.

At each p in P there is an affine function l_(u,p) on E, majorizing
all h_q(u) at q in P, and with l_(u,p)(p)=h_p(u). One can obtain it by
the finite linear-programming dual at p. To check both existence and a
finite choice, the dual feasible polyhedron consists of affine functions
l with l(q)>=h_q(u) for all q. It is nonempty, is pointed because P
affinely spans E, and has a nonempty optimal face at the finite attained
primal value. That face has a vertex, determined by r+1 affinely
independent active evaluations. Thus an optimal l is one of finitely
many affine interpolants through r+1 affinely independent base points.
Their coefficients depend continuously on u. Choosing the first
interpolant which majorizes all h_q and touches at p is Borel and
uniformly bounded on the compact normal sphere. In dimension r=0 the
constant l=h_p is the unique required choice.

Write l_(u,p)(z)=h_p(u)+s(u,p).(z-p). At a regular input w=(p,x), let
u=n_p(x). The affine inequality

    u.y <= h_p(u)+s(u,p).(q-p)                       (9)

holds for every physical point (q,y) of C, and is an equality at w.
For a barycenter-preserving row from w, the nonnegative gap in (9)
has expectation zero. More explicitly, boundedness and Borel
measurability of s and u allow them as coefficient tests in the row
moment identities (3), so the integral of that gap is zero, first on
every input restriction and hence almost everywhere. Therefore almost
every output w'=(q,y) satisfies equality in (9).

Because u.y<=h_q(u)<=l_(u,p)(q), that equality forces
u.y=h_q(u). Thus u is an outer normal of K_q at y. The target measure
is concentrated on regular boundary points, where the outer unit normal
is unique, so u=n_q(y). The coupling consequently preserves the normal
exactly, without partitioning its sphere.

Conversely a normal-preserving barycenter coupling gives all the localized
affine identities and convex inequalities by applying conditional Jensen
in each row and multiplying by any nonnegative bounded Borel function
of the preserved normal. This proves the claimed equivalence on actual
finite fiber boundaries. The argument does not apply to an arbitrary
family of boundary surfaces whose points may be interior to their
joint convex hull; actual-fiber compatibility is used in (9).
